## Statement

For the $k$th term $e_k$ of the $\operatorname{erf}$ series in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]],

$$\frac{|e_{k+1}|}{|e_k|} =\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}\frac{2k+1}{2k+3} \le\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}.$$

The displayed quotient is asserted when $e_k\ne0$. At $z=0$, every $e_k=0$, so the series and every tail are zero; the corresponding division-free inequality $|e_{k+1}|\le |z|^2|e_k|/(k+1)$ holds there as well.

Thus, if $|z|^2/(K+2)=q<1$, the tail after terms $0,\ldots,K$ is bounded by
$|e_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. The series converges locally uniformly and equals
$2/\sqrt\pi$ times the integral of $e^{-t^2}$ from $0$ to $z$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The $\operatorname{erf}$ series in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]].

[F1] [[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]]:
$e_k=(2/\sqrt\pi)(-1)^kz^{2k+1}/(k!(2k+1))$.

[F2] [[def-complex-exponential]] and
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]:
$\exp w=\sum_{k\ge0}w^k/k!$ with absolute convergence for every complex $w$.

[F3] [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]:
an entire power series may be differentiated term by term.

[F4] [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]] and
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: the real and imaginary parts of a
continuously differentiable path satisfy the fundamental theorem of calculus;
continuous derivatives on a compact parameter interval are integrable.

## Proof
1.1 For $z\ne0$, every term in [F1] is nonzero, so dividing successive absolute terms gives the stated ratio. At $z=0$ all terms vanish, and the stated division-free inequality and zero tail follow directly without division. For $k\ge K+1$ it is at most $q<1$, so the tail is dominated by $|e_{K+1}|\sum_{j\ge0}q^j=|e_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. On every disk the ratio is eventually below $1$, proving local uniform convergence. [F1, algebra]


2.1 The series in [F1] has infinite radius by step 1.1, so [F3] gives $$\operatorname{erf}'(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k}}{k!}=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\exp(-z^2),$$ using [F2] and the definition of the exponential series. Thus erf is an entire primitive of the stated integrand and $\operatorname{erf}(0)=0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]


3.1 Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C$ be any piecewise continuously differentiable path with $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma(1)=z$. On a smooth piece, put $\eta_h=\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)$. Complex differentiability gives $\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s)+\eta_h)-\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s)) =\operatorname{erf}'(\gamma(s))\eta_h+\eta_h\epsilon(\eta_h)$ with $\epsilon(\eta)\to0$ as $\eta\to0$; take $\epsilon(0)=0$. Since $\eta_h/h\to\gamma'(s)$, division by $h$ makes the remainder tend to zero and proves $(\operatorname{erf}\circ\gamma)'(s)=\operatorname{erf}'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. The derivative is continuous on that compact piece and its real and imaginary parts are integrable by [F4]. Applying [F4] componentwise and adding over the finitely many pieces gives $$\int_{\gamma}\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}e^{-t^2}\,dt=\operatorname{erf}(z)-\operatorname{erf}(0)=\operatorname{erf}(z).$$ This proves the segment identity and path independence without interchanging a series limit with a line integral. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the terms $c_k$ of $C$ and $s_k$ of $S$ in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]],

$$\frac{|c_{k+1}|}{|c_k|}\le \frac{\pi^2|z|^4/4}{(2k+1)(2k+2)}, \qquad \frac{|s_{k+1}|}{|s_k|}\le \frac{\pi^2|z|^4/4}{(2k+2)(2k+3)}.$$

Each displayed quotient is asserted only when its denominator is nonzero. At $z=0$, every $c_k=s_k=0$, so both series and every tail are zero. The corresponding division-free inequalities obtained by multiplying by $|c_k|$ or $|s_k|$ hold for every $z$.

Once the applicable bound is at most $q<1$ for all terms after a first
omitted term, the absolute tail is bounded by that term divided by $1-q$.
Both series converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb C$ and equal the integrals
of $\cos(\pi t^2/2)$ and $\sin(\pi t^2/2)$ from $0$ to $z$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The series definitions of $C,S$ in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]].

[F1] [[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]]: $c_k=(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}
z^{4k+1}/((2k)!(4k+1))$ and
$s_k=(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}/((2k+1)!(4k+3))$.

[F2] [[def-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-functions]] and
[[thm-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-power-series]]:
complex sine and cosine are given by their entire factorial power series.

[F3] [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]:
an entire power series may be differentiated term by term.

[F4] [[thm-ftc-second-part]] and
[[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]] and
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: along each compact smooth path piece,
the real and imaginary parts of a continuously differentiable function
integrate to their endpoint differences.

## Proof
1.1 If $z=0$, all terms in [F1] vanish, and their division-free bounds and zero tails hold directly. For $z\ne0$, every term is nonzero, and taking ratios in [F1] gives $$\frac{|c_{k+1}|}{|c_k|}=\frac{\pi^2|z|^4}{4} \frac{4k+1}{(2k+1)(2k+2)(4k+5)},\qquad \frac{|s_{k+1}|}{|s_k|}=\frac{\pi^2|z|^4}{4} \frac{4k+3}{(2k+2)(2k+3)(4k+7)}.$$ The omitted factors are each less than $1$, yielding the displayed bounds. [F1, algebra]


2.1 The denominators in the bounds grow quadratically in $k$, so the ratios tend to zero; summing the resulting geometric majorant gives the stated tail bound and uniform convergence on every disk. [step 1.1, algebra]


3.1 The infinite-radius power series in [F1] may be differentiated termwise by [F3]. The resulting derivatives are $$C'(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k}}{(2k)!}=\cos(\pi z^2/2),\qquad S'(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+2}}{(2k+1)!}=\sin(\pi z^2/2),$$ where the last equalities use [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]


4.1 Both $C$ and $S$ are entire primitives of their displayed integrands. For any piecewise continuously differentiable path $\gamma$ from $0$ to $z$, put $\eta_h=\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)$ on each smooth piece. Complex differentiability gives $C(\gamma(s)+\eta_h)-C(\gamma(s))=C'(\gamma(s))\eta_h+ \eta_h\epsilon_C(\eta_h)$ with $\epsilon_C(\eta)\to0$ as $\eta\to0$; take $\epsilon_C(0)=0$. Since $\eta_h/h\to\gamma'(s)$, division by $h$ makes the remainder tend to zero, and hence $(C\circ\gamma)'(s)=C'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. The same calculation gives $(S\circ\gamma)'(s)=S'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. These derivatives are continuous on compact path pieces and integrable by [F4]. The componentwise fundamental theorem and finite additivity therefore give the endpoint differences $C(z)-C(0)=C(z)$ and $S(z)-S(0)=S(z)$. Hence the integrals are path-independent and, in particular, equal the integrals along the segment from $0$ to $z$. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Definition

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Definition

Let $\gamma=x+iy:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a rectifiable contour in the sense of [[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]] and let $f=u+iv$ be continuous on its trace, with real and imaginary parts from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Define
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz:=\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)-\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)+i\left(\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)+\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)\right),$$
where the four integrals are the real Riemann–Stieltjes integrals of [[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]. Their existence is proved in [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]. On a singleton parameter interval the integral is $0$.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Definition

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$\sin z=\frac{\exp(iz)-\exp(-iz)}{2i},\quad \cos z=\frac{\exp(iz)+\exp(-iz)}2,$$
$$\sinh z=\frac{\exp z-\exp(-z)}2,\quad \cosh z=\frac{\exp z+\exp(-z)}2.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Definition

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define the Fresnel functions and error function by

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

For every $z\in\mathbb C$,
$$\sin z=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nz^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\quad \cos z=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nz^{2n}}{(2n)!},$$
$$\sinh z=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{z^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\quad \cosh z=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{z^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$
All four series have infinite radius.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be piecewise-$C^1$ and let $f$ be continuous on its trace. Then
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=\sum_j\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}f(\gamma(t))\gamma'_j(t)\,dt,$$
and
$$\int_\gamma |f(z)|\,|dz|=\sum_j\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}|f(\gamma(t))|\,|\gamma'_j(t)|\,dt.$$
The real and imaginary parts of the first display are the published vector line integrals of $(u,-v)$ and $(v,u)$, while the second is the published scalar line integral.

actual_prerequisites.actual_statement_or_definition:
## Statement

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).
